newsitem.title: USA: Berger underscores importance of China-U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: Berger underscores importance of China-U.S. ties.

text.p: U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger underscored on Thursday the importance of U.S. ties with China, but said he did not mince words about problem areas during meetings with Chinese officials this week.

Berger spoke with public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer" after returning from a three-day trip to Beijing to lay the groundwork for a late October summit between President Bill Clinton and Chinese president Jiang Zemin.

Berger said that he raised thorny issues such as human rights, especially of political dissidents, China's arms sales to Iran, and China's bid to enter the World Trade Organization, as well as areas of mutual concern, such as the situations in North Korea and Cambodia.
But the discussions were part of a new, broader strategic dialogue emerging between the two countries.

"We have broadened the range of our discussion with China and tried to engage them in not only a discussion of specific subjects that are problems, or specific areas in which we can cooperate, but a broader strategic dialogue," Berger said.
He said the China-U.S. summit would take place in Washington in late October, followed by a visit by Clinton to China next year.

"The summit is important for both countries. This is an enormously important relationship. The way in which China evolves over the next 10 years as the largest country in the world will have an enormous impact on our future," Berger said, citing such areas as the environment or nuclear non-proliferation.

On the issue of human rights, Berger said he "made clear that this continues to be a very important issue for our administration and for the American people and that... there has been very little, if any, improvement in the political rights" of Chinese citizens.
He said human rights remained an important area of disagreement between the two countries.
China and the United States have squabbled over a range of issues, including Beijing's rival, Taiwan, human rights abuses in China and Tibet, trade and nuclear proliferation.
Berger, who met Jiang Zemin on Tuesday in the seaside resort of Beidaihe, said he also made clear that Beijing could not expect to be admitted to the WTO "simply because they're a big country."

He said he expected progress, although possibly not in the short term -- and certainly no major breakthroughs at the October summit, since it would require some internal economic restructuring and "fairly significant domestic effects" on state-owned enterprises before it could join the WTO.
Trade would be one of the topics discussed during the summit, Berger said, noting that movement toward regular summits would be helpful.

Jiang's meeting with Clinton will be the first state visit to the United States by a Chinese president since the Chinese army crushed student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 3-4, 1989.
Washington switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979. Beijing considers Taiwan a rebel province and has sought to push the island into diplomatic isolation.

Sino-U.S. ties soured in March 1996 when Washington threw its weight behind Taipei by sending aircraft carriers to waters near Taiwan where China was conducting intimidatory war games in the run-up to the island's first direct presidential elections.
